paper_title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19--23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running $24.5\times$ faster on TREC DL and $16.7\times$ faster on BRIGHT.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in document reranking, particularly through listwise methods like RankGPT (Sun et al., 2023) that autoregressively generate candidate identifiers in descending order of relevance. However, this multi-step decoding incurs substantial inference latency. 1 Figure 2 Training DecisionRank with offline rankings and on-policy feedback. frozen generative teacher supplies offline rankings for RankNet (left) and conditional feedback along the students current ranking (right). One teacher-forced forward pass provides the teachers choice distributions, which are aligned with the students scores renormalized over the remaining documents. Both objectives supervise the same first-token scores. The students scoring procedure is the same during training and inference: single forward pass produces the first-token scores used to rank all candidates. Decision models address this latency by directly predicting choices or scores without generating text, as illustrated by Jev (Almeida, 2026) and AnyJev (Zhang et al., 2026a). In document reranking, single-token methods such as FIRST (Gangi Reddy et al., 2024) follow the same principle: they sort first-token document-ID logits to obtain the ranking. Training these scores to capture the ranking preferences of capable generative teachers is therefore critical to effective single-token reranking. Conventionally, ranking knowledge is transferred by training the student on static rankings generated offline by the teacher (Sun et al., 2023; Gangi Reddy et al., 2024; Schlatt et al., 2025) via learning-to-rank objectives. However, such fixed supervision cannot adapt to the students evolving predictions, leaving the teacher unable to provide feedback on the students current ranking decisions. While on-policy distillation (OPD) provides dynamic, state-aware feedback and has demonstrated notable success in autoregressive generation (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024), effectively enabling it to complement offline ranking supervision in single-token rerankers remains challenging due to the structural mismatch between sequential feedback and single-pass scoring. Specifically, standard token-level OPD relies on autoregressive rollouts to obtain conditional teacher feedback, whereas single-token reranker represents the entire ranking through static score vector in single forward pass. Given this discrepancy, naive distillation strategies are insufficient: matching only the teachers firsttoken distribution captures initial preferences but leaves subsequent conditional choices unused, while training the student to generate full ranking sequences creates mismatch with the first-token scores used at inference. This raises our core question: How can we distill the sequential ranking preferences of an autoregressive teacher into student that ranks all candidates in single forward pass? To address this question, we propose DecisionRank, decision reranking model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (Figure 2). Rather than relying on autoregressive student rollouts, we sort the students first-token scores to construct ranking prefixes from its current top-K candidates. frozen generative teacher evaluates these prefixes in single teacher-forced forward pass, providing conditional choice distributions over the remaining candidates at each ranking step. We obtain the corresponding student distributions 2 by normalizing its first-token scores over the same remaining candidates, and align them with the teacher distributions using reverse KullbackLeibler (KL) divergence in item space. This directly supervises the students first-token scores used for inference, while allowing teacher feedback to adapt as the students ranking evolves. Because the alignment operates over candidate identities rather than vocabulary tokens, the teacher and student need not share vocabulary or model architecture. We jointly optimize this on-policy objective with offline RankNet supervision derived from teacher-generated rankings, combining global ordering preferences with conditional feedback on the students current ranking. At inference, the student preserves its single-pass efficiency, ranking the full candidate set without autoregressive generation. We conduct extensive experiments across four benchmarks covering both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval tasks. Our method achieves strong effectivenesslatency tradeoff compared with existing LLMbased rerankers. As shown in Figure 1, all three distilled students (1.7B, 4B, and 8B) outperform the 27B generative teacher on TREC DL1923 (Craswell et al., 2020, 2025). Notably, our 8B student also surpasses the listwise DirectRank-8B while running 24.5 faster on TREC DL under the same input length settings. Our method consistently improves ranking effectiveness over offline RankNet supervision across all four benchmarks and outperforms alternative training objectives, including Offline KL, autoregressive SFT, autoregressive OPD, and Listwise GRPO (Shao et al., 2024; Prabhakar et al., 2026). Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary benefits of offline RankNet supervision and on-policy distillation, with their combination achieving the strongest performance. Beyond ranking effectiveness, our 8B students yield lower pairwise calibration error than their Qwen3.8 and Gemma teachers on TREC DL and BRIGHT, without calibration-specific training objective (Section 3.2.3). The contributions of this paper are threefold: We introduce item-space on-policy distillation and combine it with offline ranking supervision to distill the ranking ability of generative LLM teachers into DecisionRank, decision model for document reranking. We show that DecisionRank achieves competitive performance across general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks, with substantially lower inference latency than generative listwise rerankers. We demonstrate generalizability across teacher families and student sizes, with consistent improvements over zero-shot students across all 4 benchmarks.

sections.title: 2 Method
sections.content: DecisionRank is decision model for document reranking that learns from generative teacher. It combines offline ranking supervision with on-policy feedback (Figure 2). In this section, we describe the 3 key components of our method. First-Token Ranking and Item-Space Alignment uses first-token document-ID logits as ranking scores and aligns teacher and student choice distributions over the same candidate items. On-Policy Conditional Feedback uses the students current ranking as sequence of document selections. The teacher evaluates the remaining documents given those already selected, providing feedback to supervise the students scores. Offline Supervision and Joint Training combines this feedback with global ordering preferences from offline teacher rankings.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: We organize our experiments around four research questions: RQ1. How does our method compare with existing rerankers? RQ2. Which training objective works best for ranking with first-token logits? RQ3. Does combining offline and on-policy supervision improve ranking? RQ4. Does our method generalize across teachers and student sizes?

sections.title: 3.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: 3.1.1 Training Training data. We train on 10,000 MS MARCO queries from Rank-DistiLLM (Schlatt et al., 2025) and 6,000 synthetic queries from ReasonEmbed (Chen et al., 2026). For ReasonEmbed, we sample 500 queries from each of the 12 categories in the released dataset. For Rank-DistiLLM, we rerank the candidate documents with the corresponding teacher to construct offline ranking supervision. Students and teachers. Our students are initialized from Qwen3 at 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters (Yang et al., 2025). Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) serves as the teacher for the main experiments. All teachers remain frozen and provide both offline rankings and on-policy feedback. To evaluate generalizability across teachers, we also distill from Gemma-4-31B (Gemma Team, 2026) and ReasonRank-32B (Liu et al., 2026) (Section 3.5). Training and inference details are provided in Appendix A. 3.1.2 Evaluation Benchmarks and candidates. We evaluate reranking effectiveness on 4 benchmarks spanning general and reasoning-intensive retrieval. 1 General retrieval benchmarks. We evaluate on the 5 TREC DL years from DL19 to DL23 (Craswell et al., 2020, 2025), using the MS MARCO passage collections (Bajaj et al., 2018): DL1920 use the v1 collection and DL2123 use v2. To assess out-of-domain general retrieval, we evaluate on 7 BEIR datasets (Thakur et al., 2021): TREC-COVID, NFCorpus, DBPedia, SciFact, Signal-1M, TREC-News, and Robust04. Both TREC DL and BEIR use BM25 top-100 candidates. 2 Reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks. BRIGHT comprises 12 tasks spanning diverse domains (Su et al., 2025). We use top-100 candidates retrieved by ReasonIR-8B (Shao et al., 2025) with the released GPT-4 reasoning queries, while rerankers receive the original query. R2MED evaluates out-of-domain transfer to medical reasoning retrieval across 8 datasets (Zhang et al., 2026b), using top-100 candidates retrieved by E5-Mistral-7B-Instruct (Wang et al., 2024). sections.title: 3.2 RQ1: How does our method compare with existing rerankers?
sections.content: We compare our method with pointwise and listwise rerankers. Pointwise methods score each querydocument pair independently, while listwise methods consider multiple documents together. We evaluate ranking effectiveness across all 4 benchmarks, then examine inference efficiency and score calibration on TREC DL and BRIGHT. 6 3.2.1 Ranking Effectiveness Table 1 compares our three student sizes with existing rerankers on general retrieval and reasoning-intensive retrieval. We also include Jev (Almeida, 2026) (jev-1.14.0) through its pointwise Score and listwise Choice interfaces. Score ranks documents by expected relevance grade, while Choice ranks all 100 candidates by their returned choice probabilities. General retrieval. All three student sizes outperform the compared baselines on both TREC DL and BEIR. Our 8B student improves over the strongest baseline, listwise DirectRank, by 1.42 points on TREC DL and 2.20 points on BEIR. The advantage already appears at 1.7B: our smallest student exceeds every compared baseline on both benchmark averages, including models with up to 32B parameters. Reasoning-intensive retrieval. Our 8B student achieves the highest average score on BRIGHT, and both 4B and 8B students outperform all open-weight pointwise baselines on BRIGHT and R2MED. The 8B student reaches 36.86 on BRIGHT, improving over listwise DirectRank by 0.99 points. On R2MED, it achieves 43.55, compared with 44.50 for listwise DirectRank. With just 16,000 training queries, our method distills the teachers ability to rerank reasoning-intensive queries and transfers this ability to out-of-domain medical retrieval. 3.2.2 Inference Efficiency Figure 3 compares ranking effectiveness against single-query latency on TREC DL and BRIGHT to assess the efficiency of full-list reranking. On BRIGHT, our 4B student offers comparable ranking effectiveness and latency to Jevs listwise mode. sections.title: 3.3 RQ2: Which training objective works best for ranking with first-token logits?
sections.content: Here, we ask which form of teacher supervision best improves the first-token reranking scores used at inference. We compare five additional objectives on top of common RankNet loss: offline logit distillation (Offline KL), autoregressive supervised fine-tuning (AR SFT), autoregressive on-policy distillation (AR OPD), Listwise GRPO, and our item-space on-policy distillation (Item-space OPD). RankNet. RankNet is classic pairwise learning-to-rank loss (Burges et al., 2005). Following FIRST (Gangi Reddy et al., 2024), we use weighted RankNet objective (Equation 6) as the foundation for distillation. The following objectives each add different form of supervision to this common foundation. + Offline KL. Offline KL matches the students first-token distribution to fixed teacher distribution. Before training, we run the teacher on the full candidate set and cache its first-position distribution over candidate IDs. We then minimize forward KL, DKL(pT pS), with both distributions normalized over all candidate IDs at temperature 1. 8 + Autoregressive SFT (AR SFT). AR SFT teaches the student to generate the teachers ranking as an autoregressive sequence. We apply teacher-forced cross-entropy to the ranking tokens, following the joint ranking and language-model supervision in FIRST (Gangi Reddy et al., 2024). When prompted to rank 100 candidates in single response, LLMs produce incomplete or invalid rankings for most queries. We therefore only generate the first 20 candidate IDs from the teachers offline ranking and use them as the SFT target. The student learns to generate this ranking sequence while RankNet loss supervises the full candidate set on the first token logits. + Autoregressive OPD (AR OPD). AR OPD applies distillation at each candidate-ID position in studentgenerated ranking, following the GKD paradigm (Agarwal et al., 2024). The student first generates 20 distinct candidate rankings autoregressively. We provide the teacher with the query and the selected candidates, and append the student-generated ranking as teacher-forced response. At each ID position, both models predict the next candidate conditioned on the same student-generated prefix. We minimize reverse KL, DKL(pSpT ), between the students and teachers next-ID distributions at steps 119, with both distributions renormalized over the remaining IDs within the sampled set of 20. + Listwise GRPO. Listwise GRPO optimizes student-sampled rankings with an nDCG@10 reward, aligning with the final evaluation metric. The teachers offline ranking provides the reference for computing this reward. We adapt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) to ranking, drawing on the ranking-policy formulation of Prabhakar et al. (2026). sections.title: 4.1 Efficient LLM-based Reranking
sections.content: Generative listwise rerankers, such as RankGPT (Sun et al., 2023) and RankZephyr (Pradeep et al., 2023), produce rankings autoregressively, incurring decoding latency and repeated model calls for long candidate lists. TourRank (Chen et al., 2025a) and GroupRank (Long et al., 2026) improve efficiency through grouped 11 comparisons and parallel processing. In contrast, FIRST (Gangi Reddy et al., 2024) eliminates rankingsequence generation by sorting first-token document-ID logits, with subsequent work extending this approach (Chen et al., 2025b). Our work builds on first-token ranking and focuses on learning these scores from generative teacher.

sections.title: 4.2 Knowledge Distillation for Reranking
sections.content: Knowledge distillation transfers ranking knowledge from powerful teachers to smaller models. RankZephyr (Pradeep et al., 2023) and LiT5-Distill (Tamber et al., 2023) train generative rerankers on teacher-generated rankings, while Rank-DistiLLM (Schlatt et al., 2025) distills teacher rankings into cross-encoders using learning-to-rank objectives. DeAR (Abdallah et al., 2025) further incorporates reasoning-based supervision. Beyond offline distillation, GKD (Agarwal et al., 2024) and MiniLLM (Gu et al., 2024) leverage teacher feedback on student-generated sequences. Unlike these autoregressive approaches, DecisionRank applies on-policy teacher feedback directly to first-token ranking scores.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced DecisionRank, decision reranking model that combines offline ranking supervision with item-space on-policy distillation. Conditional teacher feedback on the students current ranking directly trains the first-token scores used at inference. This approach improves ranking across general and reasoning-intensive retrieval and generalizes across teacher families and student sizes. On TREC DL and BRIGHT, our 8B model outperforms its generative listwise counterpart with substantially lower latency. DecisionRank learns from generative teachers sequential ranking decisions while reranking the full candidate set through single-token scoring, offering promising path to distilling efficient decision models for broader applications.
